title: A smartwatch alert for a fast irregular heart rate leads to a defibrillator implant, and the X-ray after the procedure reveals a lung cancer that surgeons remove
summary: A smartwatch of unstated brand alerted a 58-year-old man to an irregular heart rate above 180 beats per minute; the care that followed found a lung adenocarcinoma, which surgeons removed.
account: Cole, Kar, Nimako and Smelt published the case in JRSM Open on 4 January 2022 without dating the alert, the defibrillator implant or the lobectomy. They work at St George's Healthcare NHS Trust (thoracic surgery) and East Surrey Hospital (respiratory medicine) in England's National Health Service (NHS). A previously well 58-year-old non-smoker was alerted by his smartwatch that his heart rate was irregular and exceeding 180 beats per minute, while he felt nothing. A 12-lead electrocardiogram by his general practitioner showed tachycardia without arrhythmia, and he was admitted. Inpatient ECGs showed incomplete right bundle branch block and intermittent first-degree atrioventricular block, and they captured no significant arrhythmia. From the smartwatch results, the cardiologist diagnosed non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, and an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator was inserted. The chest X-ray after the procedure, taken to exclude pneumothorax, incidentally showed an abnormality in the right upper zone. Computed tomography found a 28 mm lesion. Positron emission tomography showed nodes that took up fluorodeoxyglucose, and biopsy showed lepidic adenocarcinoma, staged cT1c N0 M0. He had a video-assisted right upper lobectomy with node dissection and was discharged on day 10. The 35 mm tumor was staged pT2a pN0 M0 with clear margins. The nodes showed sarcoidosis, and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging found no cardiac sarcoid. The watch's brand and model are not stated. The authors call this the first reported case of a smartwatch assisting the diagnosis of both non-sustained ventricular tachycardia and lung adenocarcinoma. In a similar case reported in November 2019 by Lausanne emergency physicians, an electrocardiogram recorded on a patient's Apple Watch showed ventricular tachycardia after standard hospital tests were unremarkable.
purpose: Alert the wearer to an irregular or fast heart rate. The lung cancer was found incidentally on the X-ray taken after the defibrillator procedure that the alert set in motion.

brief: In a case report published on 4 January 2022, clinicians at St George's Healthcare NHS Trust and East Surrey Hospital in England describe how a smartwatch alert led indirectly to a diagnosis of lung cancer. A previously well 58-year-old man with no significant smoking history received an alert from his smartwatch that his heart rate was irregular and above 180 beats per minute, while he felt nothing.[1] Electrocardiograms in hospital captured no significant arrhythmia, and a cardiologist diagnosed non-sustained ventricular tachycardia from the watch's results. He received an implantable defibrillator. The routine chest X-ray after the procedure happened to show an abnormality in his right upper lung. Further imaging and a biopsy showed an adenocarcinoma, which surgeons removed with clear margins. The cancer lay outside what the watch was built to detect. The authors judge that without the watch the tumor would likely have grown undetected and that curative surgery might not have been an option.[2] The report does not name the watch's brand or model, so its alerting algorithm cannot be identified. It gives no dates for any of the events and no follow-up beyond his discharge on the tenth day after surgery and an outpatient magnetic resonance scan of his heart.

fields.summary: A smartwatch of unstated brand alerted a 58-year-old man to an irregular heart rate above 180 beats per minute; the care that followed found a lung adenocarcinoma, which surgeons removed.
fields.account: Cole, Kar, Nimako and Smelt published the case in JRSM Open on 4 January 2022 without dating the alert, the defibrillator implant or the lobectomy. They work at St George's Healthcare NHS Trust (thoracic surgery) and East Surrey Hospital (respiratory medicine) in England's National Health Service (NHS). A previously well 58-year-old non-smoker was alerted by his smartwatch that his heart rate was irregular and exceeding 180 beats per minute, while he felt nothing. A 12-lead electrocardiogram by his general practitioner showed tachycardia without arrhythmia, and he was admitted. Inpatient ECGs showed incomplete right bundle branch block and intermittent first-degree atrioventricular block, and they captured no significant arrhythmia. From the smartwatch results, the cardiologist diagnosed non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, and an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator was inserted. The chest X-ray after the procedure, taken to exclude pneumothorax, incidentally showed an abnormality in the right upper zone. Computed tomography found a 28 mm lesion. Positron emission tomography showed nodes that took up fluorodeoxyglucose, and biopsy showed lepidic adenocarcinoma, staged cT1c N0 M0. He had a video-assisted right upper lobectomy with node dissection and was discharged on day 10. The 35 mm tumor was staged pT2a pN0 M0 with clear margins. The nodes showed sarcoidosis, and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging found no cardiac sarcoid. The watch's brand and model are not stated. The authors call this the first reported case of a smartwatch assisting the diagnosis of both non-sustained ventricular tachycardia and lung adenocarcinoma. In a similar case reported in November 2019 by Lausanne emergency physicians, an electrocardiogram recorded on a patient's Apple Watch showed ventricular tachycardia after standard hospital tests were unremarkable.
